mos-active-load.limits: Include active-load bias drift, mirror ratio and drain-voltage mismatch. Output capacitance controls how quickly an imbalance moves the node before feedback corrects it.
mos-active-load.sources: Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, §§3.2 and 3.6; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, bias, transconductance and gain stages

mos-source-follower.title: Supply feedthrough and signal gain use different numerators
mos-source-follower.setup: At independently established valid follower bias points, use $g_m=2$ mS, $g_{mb}=0.4$ mS and $g_{ds}=20$ μS. The bulk is grounded. Compare AC load conductance while treating these local parameters as fixed.
analysis: Heavier loading slightly reduces supply feedthrough in this local model, but it reduces signal gain at the same time. The improvement is not free supply rejection. Body transconductance reduces signal following even with an open signal load and separately retained bias current.

A physical load change may alter DC current, transconductance and threshold. The table deliberately compares fixed local models; to predict the same hardware after changing its DC load, first recompute its operating point.
mos-source-follower.limits: Include bias-sink conductance and noise, input-source impedance and supply capacitance. This is a low-frequency derivative, not a wideband PSRR claim.
mos-source-follower.sources: Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, §§3.2 and 3.6; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, bias, transconductance and gain stages

mos-current-loaded-follower.title: Sink noise appears at the output impedance
mos-current-loaded-follower.setup: A follower has 500 Ω local output resistance including its bias sink and signal load. Compare uncorrelated white current noise injected by the sink over a rectangular 10 kHz band.
analysis: An ideal current-sink symbol omits a potentially important noise source. Increasing follower transconductance lowers node impedance and this conversion, but costs bias power. The follower’s own channel noise, source resistor noise and gate-source noise still contribute.

Noise also depends on frequency-dependent node impedance. A capacitive load rolls off some output noise but may alter stability and settling; the effective integration bandwidth then differs from the rectangular band assumed here.
mos-current-loaded-follower.limits: Use the actual sink’s noise model and combine powers at a common reference. Do not treat DC current accuracy as evidence of low noise.
mos-current-loaded-follower.sources: Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, §§3.2 and 3.6; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, bias, transconductance and gain stages

mos-common-gate.title: A 50 Ω entrance requires substantial transconductance
mos-common-gate.setup: Use ideal common-gate stages without body effect or output conductance, a 1 kΩ drain load and a 50 Ω signal-generator resistance. Compare independently chosen devices at 0.2 V overdrive and a 5 V supply.
analysis: The respective bias currents are 0.2, 1 and 2 mA, giving nominal path powers 1, 5 and 10 mW. Matching the input to 50 Ω consumes current and attenuates the source voltage by half at that input. The local source-to-drain gain is not the generator gain.

At fixed overdrive, these gm choices require different geometry/current density; they are not three gate settings of one unchanged transistor at identical current. At radio frequencies package and input capacitance modify the impedance.
mos-common-gate.limits: Check DC load-line headroom: the 2 mA row drops 2 V across the 1 kΩ drain load. Include noise, parasitics and the source’s actual impedance across the band.
mos-common-gate.sources: Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, §§3.2 and 3.6; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, bias, transconductance and gain stages

mos-cascode-amplifier.title: Two-sided cascodes can leave almost no output window
mos-cascode-amplifier.setup: A simplified telescopic output has two equal-overdrive NMOS devices below the output and two equal-overdrive PMOS devices above it. Use a 3.3 V rail, independently generated wide-swing biases and no additional margin.
analysis: High intrinsic gain can coexist with an unusably narrow signal window. Lower overdrive recovers swing but generally requires more device area at a fixed current, adding capacitance. A folded topology rearranges headroom but introduces its own current and noise costs.

The gate-bias generators may impose additional supply requirements beyond the output-stack inequalities. Check the reference network, input common-mode range and internal nodes before accepting the apparently broad low-overdrive row.
mos-cascode-amplifier.limits: Add mismatch, body effect and intentional saturation margin. The table is a minimal stack estimate, not a complete op-amp rail-range specification.
mos-cascode-amplifier.sources: Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, §§3.2 and 3.6; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, bias, transconductance and gain stages

mos-differential-pair.title: Symmetry cancels second harmonic but leaves third harmonic
mos-differential-pair.setup: A matched un-degenerated MOS pair has balanced overdrive 0.5 V and a fixed tail. Consider its differential current output under a small sinusoidal differential input, with both devices saturated.
analysis: The matched differential output is an odd function, so its ideal second-order term cancels. This does not make it perfectly linear. A single branch voltage or a mismatched load can recover even-order distortion, and an active mirror introduces additional asymmetry.

The estimates are the cubic expansion, not an exact harmonic analysis. Use the complete steering law to verify larger signals and keep drain and tail compliance separate from the distortion calculation.
mos-differential-pair.limits: Include mismatch, finite tail resistance and load nonlinearity. Common-mode motion can modulate bias and distortion even when the differential signal is small.
mos-differential-pair.sources: Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, §§3.2 and 3.6; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, bias, transconductance and gain stages

mos-differential-range.title: Rejection must be compared with signal size
mos-differential-range.setup: A measurement has 2 V common-mode interference and only 1 mV wanted differential signal. Compare equivalent input leakage for a system CMRR specified as a voltage ratio, assuming the circuit stays within common-mode range.
analysis: A large decibel figure may still be inadequate when common mode dwarfs the signal. Choose CMRR from the actual interference-to-signal ratio and required error, then allocate mismatch between devices, loads, tail and external networks.

The same rejection figure must hold at the interference frequency. DC CMRR may deteriorate through capacitance mismatch or tail impedance. Input headroom is a separate prerequisite: no rejection calculation saves a pair whose tail or input devices are outside their valid region.
mos-differential-range.limits: Check input protection and source impedance symmetry. Translate every CMRR claim into an input error before comparing it with the sensor resolution.
mos-differential-range.sources: Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, §§3.2 and 3.6; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, bias, transconductance and gain stages

mos-mirror-loaded-differential.title: The mirrored signal path carries its own pole
mos-mirror-loaded-differential.setup: The mirror’s diode-connected gate node has approximately 1 mS conductance. Compare total capacitance at that node. Ignore other poles to isolate the delay of the left-branch contribution.
analysis: Only the mirrored contribution sees this pole; the direct right-branch current reaches the output through a different path. Their sum therefore changes in amplitude and phase, rather than simply becoming one identical-pole signal. High-frequency common-mode conversion can also grow when the paths cease to balance.

Larger mirror devices can improve matching or reduce flicker noise but add gate capacitance. More current raises gm and moves the pole upward at a power cost. Evaluate those changes together with output-node capacitance and gain.
mos-mirror-loaded-differential.limits: The node conductance includes output conductance and any reference network in a fuller model. Include parasitic coupling and bias-source impedance.
mos-mirror-loaded-differential.sources: Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, §§3.2 and 3.6; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, bias, transconductance and gain stages

mos-differential-degeneration.title: Linearity, resistor noise and common-mode voltage share one choice
mos-differential-degeneration.setup: A pair carries a 2 mA tail, has balanced gm = 2 mS and uses equal source resistors. Threshold and overdrive are each 1 V; tail compliance is 0.3 V. Compare resistor thermal noise at 300 K, ignoring transistor noise.
analysis: Balanced lower common-mode bounds become 2.3, 2.8 and 4.3 V because each resistor carries 1 mA. The last choice can leave little range on a 5 V supply even though it gives strong local linearization. Resistor noise does not disappear when gain is reduced.

The differential resistor-noise estimate uses two independent resistors and input referral through the local source feedback. A complete stage also includes channel, load and tail noise and their transfer factors.
mos-differential-degeneration.limits: Check resistor matching and temperature coefficients as well as noise. A split-tail or other degeneration topology changes DC drop and must be analyzed from its actual connections.
mos-differential-degeneration.sources: Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, §§3.2 and 3.6; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, bias, transconductance and gain stages

mos-complementary-output.title: A capacitive load demands alternating current at zero voltage crossing
mos-complementary-output.setup: A complementary buffer drives a 2 V peak sine into 1 kΩ in parallel with 10 nF. Calculate load current independently of the output transistor model.
analysis: Resistive and capacitive currents are in quadrature, so their peak amplitudes combine as a vector rather than a direct sum. At high frequency the buffer must provide its largest capacitive current near the voltage zero crossing, a region where class-AB crossover behavior matters.

Gate-driver slew, output-device transconductance and available headroom must support this current. A quiescent resistance estimate cannot establish large-signal capacitive drive. Feedback can reduce crossover error only while it retains bandwidth and stability.
mos-complementary-output.limits: Include output capacitance, driver current and device dissipation along the reactive trajectory. Check both current directions and the intended load range.
mos-complementary-output.sources: Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, §§3.2 and 3.6; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, bias, transconductance and gain stages

mos-two-stage-amplifier.title: A nulling resistor depends on second-stage gm
mos-two-stage-amplifier.setup: A two-stage amplifier uses $g_{m2}=2$ mS and a 50 pF Miller capacitor. In the simple compensated two-node model, compare a series resistor with the capacitor.
analysis: The sign of the zero matters as much as its frequency. A right-half-plane zero has the magnitude trend of a zero but adds phase lag; a left-half-plane zero can add lead. The nominal 500 Ω cancellation relies on the actual second-stage gm.

If gm changes with bias or temperature, a fixed resistor no longer cancels exactly. Check the pole and zero movement across operating points rather than treating the nominal resistor as a universal stability cure.
mos-two-stage-amplifier.limits: Include output load, capacitor parasitics and all remaining poles. Phase margin and transient settling must be verified in the complete feedback loop.
mos-two-stage-amplifier.sources: Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, §§3.2 and 3.6; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, bias, transconductance and gain stages

mos-noise-design.title: A low-frequency limit changes flicker-noise integration
mos-noise-design.setup: A device has white input density 5 nV/√Hz and a 100 Hz flicker corner, modeled as $e_n^2=e_0^2(1+f_c/f)$. Integrate up to 1 kHz with an ideal rectangular band.
analysis: The 1/f contribution grows logarithmically as the lower edge moves downward. A slow measurement’s noise budget therefore needs a defined observation time or low-frequency response. Quoting only a white density at 1 kHz can understate noise for DC sensing.

Larger input area can reduce a process-dependent flicker coefficient while increasing capacitance. Chopping can shift low-frequency errors, but introduces switching artifacts. Compare these options against the source and signal bandwidth.
mos-noise-design.limits: The single-corner model omits drift and random-telegraph behavior. Use measured spectra and the actual filter’s weighting for an instrument.
mos-noise-design.sources: Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, §§3.2 and 3.6; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, bias, transconductance and gain stages; AoE chapter 8

opamp-ideal.title: An accuracy target imposes a loop-gain target
opamp-ideal.setup: Use a finite DC open-loop gain of 100,000 and resistive noninverting feedback. Compare ideal gains while preserving a valid linear output and input range.
analysis: A single open-loop gain specification supports different accuracies at different noise gains. For approximately 0.01% finite-gain error at noise gain 100, the required open-loop gain is roughly one million, not 100,000. External resistor ratio and offset errors must be budgeted in addition.
At signal frequency, use the complex open-loop gain rather than its DC value. A perfectly derived ideal equation can overstate accuracy once loop gain falls.
opamp-ideal.limits: Check feedback polarity, input range, output current and stability first. A finite-gain correction does not repair saturation or an invalid input stage.
opamp-ideal.sources: Asadi, Applied Op Amp Circuits, feedback applications; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, error and dynamic models; Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, chapters 4, 5 and 8

opamp-dc-errors.title: A calibrated offset budget still has drift and gain terms
opamp-dc-errors.setup: A gain-100 measurement produces 1 V full-scale output. Use maximum input offset 10 μV, drift 0.2 μV/°C, bias-current source drop 10 μV and ratio error 100 ppm. Form a conservative absolute sum without assuming cancellation.
analysis: The 100 ppm ratio contribution is 0.1 mV at 1 V output, while the bias drop contributes 1 mV. These terms can dominate a nominally small offset. Calibrating initial offset can remove a repeatable value at the calibration condition but leaves drift and range-dependent behavior.

The absolute sum is appropriate for a guarantee without established correlations. A statistical root-sum-square estimate answers a different yield or uncertainty question and should not replace a worst-case limit silently.
opamp-dc-errors.limits: Add finite loop gain, reference error, source variation, noise and CMRR/PSRR where relevant. Use guaranteed limits at the intended conditions rather than mixing typical and maximum figures.
opamp-dc-errors.sources: Asadi, Applied Op Amp Circuits, feedback applications; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, error and dynamic models; Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, chapters 4, 5 and 8

opamp-ac-limits.title: Large-step time contains both a rate limit and a settling requirement
opamp-ac-limits.setup: A closed loop has 100 kHz first-order bandwidth and 0.5 V/μs slew. Compare output step sizes with a 0.1% final accuracy target. Treat slew and the linear tail as separate initial constraints.
analysis: The small step may never slew, while the large step may spend a substantial interval current limited before entering its linear tail. These columns are not an exact sum for a real transition: the boundary between regimes depends on internal state and the remaining error.

A settling specification needs step amplitude and error band. A percentage band scales with the step; an absolute half-code band from an ADC can impose a different tail requirement. Ringing and overload recovery add behavior beyond this one-pole estimate.
opamp-ac-limits.limits: Check load current and rail margin throughout the step. Small-signal bandwidth, slew and overload recovery are separate device characteristics.
opamp-ac-limits.sources: Asadi, Applied Op Amp Circuits, feedback applications; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, error and dynamic models; Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, chapters 4, 5 and 8

opamp-bjt-internals.title: Base shot noise matters for high source resistance
opamp-bjt-internals.setup: Use a simplified individual BJT input branch with beta 200 at 300 K. Estimate base-current shot-noise density as $\sqrt{2qI_B}$, without claiming this is the complete noise model of an op amp.
analysis: Increasing collector current improves transconductance and can lower voltage noise, but increases base current and this source-resistance conversion. A high-resistance source can therefore favor a different bias or input technology from a low-resistance source.

The full differential stage also includes the other input branch, current-source and mirror noise, correlations and frequency dependence. Bias cancellation circuitry can reduce average DC input current without eliminating all current-noise mechanisms.
opamp-bjt-internals.limits: Use actual amplifier noise spectra and bias specifications for a component choice. This shot-noise estimate explains one physical tradeoff rather than predicting an entire commercial device.
opamp-bjt-internals.sources: Asadi, Applied Op Amp Circuits, feedback applications; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, error and dynamic models; Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, chapters 4, 5 and 8

opamp-cmos-internals.title: Rail-to-rail output is load dependent
opamp-cmos-internals.setup: Approximate an upper common-source output device near its rail as 50 Ω on resistance on a 3.3 V supply. Compare source current, without including any extra internal headroom or current limit.
analysis: The output can approach the rail at a light load but loses substantial swing at a heavier one. A “rail-to-rail” label must be paired with the load current and guaranteed output-swing conditions. The lower device can have a different resistance and sinking behavior.

Input rail range is a separate architecture question. Complementary input pairs can cover both rails while changing total gm through their overlap region; output devices do not establish that input behavior.
opamp-cmos-internals.limits: The ohmic model is only a local near-rail estimate. Driver range, temperature, current limiting and nonlinear device behavior can make actual swing worse.
opamp-cmos-internals.sources: Asadi, Applied Op Amp Circuits, feedback applications; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, error and dynamic models; Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, chapters 4, 5 and 8

opamp-input-tradeoffs.title: Bandwidth limits white noise but may not remove drift
opamp-input-tradeoffs.setup: An illustrative amplifier has 5 nV/√Hz white input density. A first-order low-pass sets the noise bandwidth. Ignore flicker, current noise and all resistor sources for this isolated comparison.
analysis: The −3 dB corner is not a rectangular integration width. Using it directly would understate this first-order filter’s white-noise power by a factor π/2. Narrowing bandwidth helps white noise but extends settling and does not automatically eliminate offset drift.

For a high-resistance source, current noise and resistor thermal noise can outweigh the quoted voltage density. For slow sensing, include flicker noise and switching artifacts from chopper/autozero architectures over the actual measurement window.
opamp-input-tradeoffs.limits: Integrate every noise source through its own transfer function. Do not use signal gain where a different noise gain applies.
opamp-input-tradeoffs.sources: Asadi, Applied Op Amp Circuits, feedback applications; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, error and dynamic models; Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, chapters 4, 5 and 8

opamp-noninverting.title: Ratio tracking matters more than equal absolute temperature coefficients
opamp-noninverting.setup: A noninverting gain-11 stage uses a feedback ratio of 10. Both resistors change with temperature; compare differential temperature coefficients over a 50 °C change, using a first-order ratio approximation.
analysis: Two resistors with large but closely tracked temperature coefficients can preserve a ratio better than two individually stable resistors whose coefficients differ. A matched network can also reduce unequal thermal gradients, although layout and self-heating remain relevant.

The gain change scales by $(G-1)/G$ because the noninverting gain includes the constant one. At high gain this factor approaches unity; near a follower it becomes small. Offset drift and source bias-current error are separate contributions.
opamp-noninverting.limits: Check ratio tolerance, tracking over the full range, resistor voltage coefficient and unequal dissipation. Calibration at one temperature cannot remove an unknown tracking curve.
opamp-noninverting.sources: Asadi, Applied Op Amp Circuits, feedback applications; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, error and dynamic models; Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, chapters 4, 5 and 8

opamp-inverting-summing.title: A quiet channel still changes noise gain
opamp-inverting-summing.setup: An inverting mixer uses equal 20 kΩ input and feedback resistors. N channels remain connected to ideal low-impedance sources even when their signal voltage is zero. The amplifier has nominal GBW 2 MHz.
analysis: Every signal coefficient remains −1, but the loop sees the parallel input conductances. Zero signal is not the same as an open channel. A gain/bandwidth calculation that counts only currently audible or nonzero channels can therefore be wrong.

A 10 μV input offset becomes about 20, 30 or 50 μV output in these three configurations. Channel switching also changes noise gain and can inject charge into the summing node. Keeping unused channels connected to a defined impedance can make behavior more predictable.
opamp-inverting-summing.limits: Include real source resistance, switch capacitance and all resistor noise. Verify stability for every intended channel configuration.
opamp-inverting-summing.sources: Asadi, Applied Op Amp Circuits, feedback applications; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, error and dynamic models; Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, chapters 4, 5 and 8

opamp-difference.title: Common-mode rejection is an absolute error budget
opamp-difference.setup: A subtractor processes a 10 mV difference on 10 V common mode. Assume its supplies and internal input range support that common mode. Compare total system CMRR, including ratios and the amplifier.
columns: Common-mode output error at unity gain
analysis: The required ratio matching follows from the desired error, not from a generic “precision resistor” label. A four-resistor stage’s CMRR may be dominated by source resistance or ratio tracking even when the op amp itself has an excellent intrinsic specification.
At higher signal gain, refer common-mode leakage to the input before comparing it with the sensor. Frequency-dependent source and parasitic mismatch can make AC rejection worse than the DC result.
opamp-difference.limits: Internal input voltage, resistor voltage ratings and fault conditions must also be valid. Mathematical cancellation does not imply the inputs can tolerate arbitrary common mode.
opamp-difference.sources: Asadi, Applied Op Amp Circuits, feedback applications; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, error and dynamic models; Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, chapters 4, 5 and 8

opamp-instrumentation.title: High input impedance still requires a bias-current budget
opamp-instrumentation.setup: An instrumentation amplifier has total gain 200. Its two inputs see equal source Thévenin resistances, but input bias currents differ by 100 pA. Compute only the differential source-drop contribution.
opamp-instrumentation.equation: V_{error,in}=\Delta I_B R_S,\quad V_{error,out}=G\Delta I_B R_S
analysis: The source resistance can turn a tiny current mismatch into a substantial measurement offset. Equal source resistances cancel equal signed currents, not unequal currents. Source-resistance mismatch adds a term from the average bias current as well.

A low-resistance bridge and a high-resistance electrochemical sensor impose different input requirements even at the same voltage range and gain. Provide bias returns for floating sensors, then include their loading, leakage and noise in the source model.
opamp-instrumentation.limits: Check bias variation with common mode and temperature, intrinsic offset, internal swing and reference-pin impedance. High input impedance alone does not establish precision.
opamp-instrumentation.sources: Asadi, Applied Op Amp Circuits, feedback applications; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, error and dynamic models; Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, chapters 4, 5 and 8

opamp-transimpedance.title: Voltage noise rises through the capacitive noise gain
opamp-transimpedance.setup: A TIA has $R_F=1$ MΩ, $C_F=5$ pF and total input capacitance 50 pF. An equivalent input voltage-noise density is 10 nV/√Hz. Assume adequate loop gain for this isolated noise-gain comparison.
analysis: At high frequency noise gain tends toward $1+C_{in}/C_F=11$. The signal transimpedance rolls off while this voltage-noise contribution rises, so referring all noise through a constant 1 MΩ would give the wrong input-current spectrum.

The feedback resistor contributes about 128.7 nV/√Hz voltage noise at DC at 300 K before filtering, while detector shot noise and amplifier current noise follow different paths. Integrate the complete output noise before converting it to measurement uncertainty.
opamp-transimpedance.limits: Finite loop gain modifies these transfers near crossover. Include compensation, detector bias, board capacitance and leakage in the actual TIA.
opamp-transimpedance.sources: Asadi, Applied Op Amp Circuits, feedback applications; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, error and dynamic models; Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, chapters 4, 5 and 8

opamp-integrator.title: Offset sets the maximum uninterrupted integration time
opamp-integrator.setup: An ideal integrator uses $R_{IN}=10$ kΩ and $C_F=100$ nF, starts at zero output and has 2 V available swing in the relevant direction. Compare constant equivalent input errors, with no leakage resistor.
analysis: The integrator needs a time-window specification as well as a transfer function. A small offset that is harmless in a gain stage becomes an accumulating state. Reset, leakage feedback or anti-windup can bound it, but each changes measurement behavior.
Calibration can subtract an average drift slope under fixed conditions, while noise, leakage variation and dielectric absorption remain. A capacitor reset may inject charge or leave a memory tail.
opamp-integrator.limits: Include initial charge, input bias currents, capacitor leakage and output recovery. A finite-DC-gain integrator reaches a bounded equilibrium only if that equilibrium fits the output range.
opamp-integrator.sources: Asadi, Applied Op Amp Circuits, feedback applications; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, error and dynamic models; Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, chapters 4, 5 and 8

opamp-differentiator.title: Differentiation emphasizes the top of the noise band
opamp-differentiator.setup: External sensor noise has flat 10 nV/√Hz density and is passed through an ideal derivative scale $H=j2\pi f\tau$, with $\tau=100$ μs. Integrate only a rectangular band from zero to B, assumed well inside the derivative region.
analysis: Output noise grows as bandwidth to the three-halves power, rather than the square-root law of a flat-gain amplifier. This makes a derivative especially sensitive to fast sensor noise. A deliberate upper limit is part of the measurement specification.

This is external signal-path noise. The op amp’s own input voltage noise follows the circuit’s noise gain, and resistor/current-noise sources have their own paths; they cannot be substituted into this derivative formula automatically.
opamp-differentiator.limits: The practical series resistor and feedback capacitor bound the transfer. Integrate the actual band-limited response when the noise band approaches either corner.
opamp-differentiator.sources: Asadi, Applied Op Amp Circuits, feedback applications; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, error and dynamic models; Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, chapters 4, 5 and 8; Fiore, AC Electrical Circuit Analysis, Fourier and Bode methods

opamp-active-filters.title: An anti-alias target can require another pole
opamp-active-filters.setup: An ideal fourth-order Butterworth low-pass has 1 kHz cutoff. An ADC samples at 10 kHz. Compare attenuation at frequencies approaching and reaching its 5 kHz Nyquist frequency.
analysis: If the specification demands at least 60 dB at 5 kHz while retaining a 1 kHz Butterworth cutoff, four poles are insufficient in this ideal comparison. Five poles give about 69.9 dB there. Alternatively revise sampling rate, transition width or approximation, then recalculate passband and transient consequences.

Nyquist alone does not protect the measurement: out-of-band signals can fold into the wanted band. The required attenuation depends on their amplitude relative to the permitted aliased error, not only on ADC bit count.
opamp-active-filters.limits: Include component tolerance, amplifier bandwidth, internal resonant amplitude and actual ADC input loading. Filter −3 dB bandwidth and ENBW remain different quantities.
opamp-active-filters.sources: Asadi, Applied Op Amp Circuits, feedback applications; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, error and dynamic models; Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, chapters 4, 5 and 8; Van Valkenburg, Analog Filter Design, approximation and realization

opamp-precision-rectifier.title: A rectifier-based meter is not automatically true RMS
opamp-precision-rectifier.setup: A meter rectifies a waveform, averages its absolute value and scales the result to read the RMS of a sine. Compare unit-peak waveforms with zero DC offset.
analysis: The square wave reads about 11.1% high and the triangle about 3.8% low even with a perfect precision rectifier. The error comes from the chosen waveform conversion, not the diode drop. A calibrated average-responding meter and a true-RMS computation measure different quantities.
True RMS requires averaging the square and taking its root, or an equivalent thermal/algorithmic method. Crest factor, bandwidth and overload can still limit a practical RMS converter.
opamp-precision-rectifier.limits: Check the waveform family, DC contribution, rectifier recovery and filter settling. A precise half-wave or absolute-value circuit does not establish a universal AC amplitude measurement.
opamp-precision-rectifier.sources: Asadi, Applied Op Amp Circuits, feedback applications; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, error and dynamic models; Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, chapters 4, 5 and 8; Fiore, AC Electrical Circuit Analysis, §1.2

opamp-current-servo.title: Kelvin sensing keeps wiring drop out of the commanded current
opamp-current-servo.setup: A current servo commands 1 V across a nominal 10 Ω sense resistor, targeting 100 mA. In a two-wire connection, an unintended series resistance is included in the sensed drop. Compare that resistance before adopting four-wire sensing.
analysis: Feedback faithfully regulates the voltage it measures, including the unwanted wire drop. More loop gain does not correct a sense-boundary mistake. Separate sense leads can exclude most current-carrying lead resistance from the measured resistor voltage.
The sense return and amplifier reference must still share a valid low-noise reference. Ground shifts can become input errors, and remote sense wiring can add inductance or capacitance to the loop.
opamp-current-servo.limits: Include sense-resistor tolerance and heating, input offset, compliance and transistor dissipation. Kelvin sensing corrects a specific wiring error rather than the whole current budget.
opamp-current-servo.sources: Asadi, Applied Op Amp Circuits, feedback applications; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, error and dynamic models; Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, chapters 4, 5 and 8

opamp-load-stability.title: Isolation trades load accuracy for a gentler dynamic load
opamp-load-stability.setup: Feedback senses the amplifier output before an isolation resistor. The downstream load includes 1 nF capacitance and draws 1 mA DC. Compare resistor values using only the external load-side RC estimate.
analysis: A larger resistor can isolate capacitance more effectively for some amplifiers but increases the error outside local feedback and slows the load-side response. These are design costs, not failures of the ideal amplifier law.

Remote sensing can correct the DC drop but moves the downstream dynamics into the loop. A dual-path network may combine slow remote accuracy with local high-frequency feedback, requiring a fresh return-ratio analysis.
opamp-load-stability.limits: The RC times omit amplifier bandwidth, slew and current limit. Select resistance with the actual output-impedance/load guidance and verify all intended load conditions.
opamp-load-stability.sources: Asadi, Applied Op Amp Circuits, feedback applications; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, error and dynamic models; Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, chapters 4, 5 and 8

opamp-function-design.title: More converter bits do not remove analog noise
opamp-function-design.setup: A 3.3 V full-scale ADC follows an analog chain with gain 100. Compare ideal quantization step and its uniform-error RMS referred to the sensor, assuming a sufficiently varying signal and no other converter errors.
analysis: If the analog chain already contributes 1 μV RMS input noise, the 12-bit quantization estimate is larger than that noise, while the 16-bit case is much smaller. Moving to 20 ideal bits barely improves the complete noise floor unless analog noise is reduced too. Offset, drift and gain accuracy remain separate limits.

The uniform quantization-noise model can fail for static or correlated signals, and real converters have reference noise, nonlinearity and effective-resolution limits. Oversampling helps only under suitable noise and bandwidth conditions.
opamp-function-design.limits: Allocate analog range, gain, filtering, reference and acquisition settling before interpreting code count as measurement accuracy.
opamp-function-design.sources: Asadi, Applied Op Amp Circuits, feedback applications; Huijsing, Operational Amplifiers, error and dynamic models; Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, chapters 4, 5 and 8; Selvam, Analog Function Circuits, measurement functions; AoE chapter 13

precision-references.title: Reference drift at three input levels
precision-references.setup: A 4.096 V, 16-bit ADC sees a fixed input. Its reference rises by 80 ppm after calibration. Use the first-order ratio model; one code is 62.5 μV.
analysis: The error grows with input because the reference changes the ruler. It is a slope error, not a fixed input offset.
At zero input this contribution vanishes in the ideal ratio model, although ADC offset, amplifier drift and reference-return disturbances can still produce nonzero readings.
precision-references.limits: Use the exact transfer function at endpoints. A single calibration coefficient does not remove later temperature drift.
precision-references.sources: The Art of Electronics, third edition, §9.10 and Chapter 5

precision-noise-grounding.title: Bandwidth as a noise and speed budget
precision-noise-grounding.setup: A white input density of 10 nV/√Hz is filtered by a first-order unity low-pass. Compare cutoffs; settling is to 1% after a step.
analysis: A decade more bandwidth gives √10 more noise and ten times faster first-order settling.
The comparison excludes flicker noise and drift. At sufficiently low cutoff, those mechanisms replace white noise as the limiting error.
precision-noise-grounding.limits: An additional ADC digital filter changes both the equivalent noise bandwidth and latency.
precision-noise-grounding.sources: The Art of Electronics, Chapter 8, especially §§8.14–8.16

precision-calibration.title: Excitation current versus sensor self-heating
precision-calibration.setup: A 100 Ω sensor has local slope 0.385 Ω/K and thermal rise 0.4 K/mW. Compare constant-current excitation. Voltage noise is not included.
analysis: Sensitivity grows linearly with excitation while heating grows quadratically. The best current depends on voltage noise and thermal mounting.
Pulsed excitation may reduce average heating, but electrical acquisition and thermal transients must be analyzed before relying on duty cycle.
precision-calibration.limits: The thermal coefficient is a teaching assumption and must be measured or specified for the installed sensor.
precision-calibration.sources: The Art of Electronics, Chapters 5 and 8; original sensor and calibration examples

power-linear-regulators.title: Three input rails for one linear load
power-linear-regulators.setup: A 3.3 V output draws 0.2 A. Ignore quiescent loss and use 60 K/W board thermal resistance at 30 °C ambient.
analysis: Lower input headroom reduces heat, but it also reduces dropout margin and may reduce ripple rejection.
At 12 V the estimated junction may exceed the intended operating limit even though output current remains only 200 mA.
power-linear-regulators.limits: Thermal resistance is board dependent. Validate the low-input dropout corner separately from the high-input heat corner.

power-buck-converters.title: One inductor, three load currents
power-buck-converters.setup: Ideal 12-to-5 V buck, 22 μH, 500 kHz. CCM ripple is 0.26515 A. Compare the requested CCM waveform; the diode stage cannot carry negative current.
analysis: Ripple is set by voltages, inductance and timing, not by load in this CCM approximation. Changing load shifts the waveform vertically.
Below the boundary a diode stage gains a zero-current interval; fixed-duty output now depends on load.
power-buck-converters.limits: Do not use the negative-current CCM estimate to claim an asynchronous stage returns energy to its input.
power-buck-converters.sources: The Art of Electronics, §9.6.5; TI SLVA477

power-boost-isolated.title: Lower input increases boost switch current
power-boost-isolated.setup: An ideal boost holds 12 V at 0.5 A, with 22 μH and 500 kHz in CCM. Compute current at three input voltages.
analysis: Output power is fixed at 6 W, so average input current rises as input voltage falls.
Lower input is often the peak-current corner. Voltage stress and thermal loss need their own checks over the full range.
power-boost-isolated.limits: Efficiency, saturation, current-limit tolerance and switch/diode drops are excluded.
power-boost-isolated.sources: The Art of Electronics, §§9.6.6–9.6.10; TI SLVA372

power-control-layout.title: Compensation changes cycle-to-cycle current error
power-control-layout.setup: Ideal peak-current loop with m₁ = 0.2 A/μs and m₂ = 0.4 A/μs. Compare added slopes.
analysis: This mechanism is sampled at switching frequency and differs from the outer voltage-loop phase margin.
A stable inner loop still needs an appropriate outer compensation and operating-range test.
power-control-layout.limits: Actual controllers may use internal adaptive compensation; inspect the architecture and sense scaling.
power-control-layout.sources: The Art of Electronics, §9.6; original sampled-ramp derivation; TI implementation notes

rf-impedance-matching.title: Resistance mismatch on a 50 Ω port
rf-impedance-matching.setup: Purely resistive loads terminate a lossless 50 Ω line. Compare reflection magnitude and return loss.
analysis: A low resistance returns an inverted voltage wave; a high resistance returns a wave of the same polarity.
Perfect matching eliminates the ideal reflected wave, but real fixtures, frequency-dependent parasitics and measurement uncertainty set finite measured limits.
rf-impedance-matching.limits: The power interpretation assumes real positive reference impedance and no line loss.
rf-impedance-matching.sources: Fiore, AC Electrical Circuit Analysis; ADI matching tutorial; original wave-boundary example

rf-signal-chains.title: LNA gain versus receiver noise figure
rf-signal-chains.setup: An LNA has 1.5 dB NF and adjustable teaching gain. It precedes a mixer of −6 dB gain / 6 dB NF and IF amplifier of 30 dB gain / 5 dB NF. All ports use consistent noise definitions.
analysis: More initial gain suppresses the input-referred contribution of later stages; returns diminish as total NF approaches the LNA’s own factor.
Each additional 10 dB of LNA gain also raises blocker power into the mixer by 10 dB, potentially making compression the limiting condition.
rf-signal-chains.limits: Real gain changes can also change LNA NF and intercept; this teaching comparison holds them fixed.
rf-signal-chains.sources: The Art of Electronics, Chapter 8 and §13.13; ADI RF application notes

transmission-lines.title: First arrival versus final divider
transmission-lines.setup: A 1 V source with 10 Ω source resistance drives a lossless 50 Ω line. Compare resistive loads.
analysis: A matched load makes first arrival equal final DC even when the source is mismatched, because no load reflection returns.
A high-resistance load can initially overshoot its final voltage, followed by corrections at odd multiples of flight time.
transmission-lines.limits: Real driver nonlinearity, clamps and line loss alter the bounce sequence.
transmission-lines.sources: The Art of Electronics, §§12.9–12.10 and Appendix H

differential-pairs.title: Skew creates a common-mode pulse
differential-pairs.setup: Opposite linear transitions each move 0.4 V in 1 ns. Compare delays smaller than rise time.
analysis: The differential pair generates common mode internally when its paths are delayed unequally; external noise need not be present.
A resistor only across the pair terminates odd mode. Common-mode energy sees a different boundary and can continue to reflect.
differential-pairs.limits: The linear-ramp model excludes modal dispersion, amplitude imbalance and receiver clamps.
differential-pairs.sources: The Art of Electronics, §12.10; TI SNLA302; original coupled-line and skew derivations

sampling-converter-errors.title: Resolution increases the acquisition requirement
sampling-converter-errors.setup: Full-span first-order acquisition with 1 kΩ source and 20 pF capacitance. Require residual below half a code.
analysis: The exponential needs more time for smaller residual, but each additional bit adds only ln2 times RC in this first-order model.
A real driver can have a long nonlinear settling tail that invalidates this simple scaling.
sampling-converter-errors.limits: Sample-switch resistance, parasitics, kickback and reference recovery are excluded.
sampling-converter-errors.sources: The Art of Electronics, Chapter 13; ADI MT-001; original acquisition example
